articles.title: An eye on Balochistan border
articles.content: THE intensifying Yemeni Houthistrikeson Saudi Arabia have triggered a debate over thepossible activation of the Makkah accord. Statements and clarifications about possible and emerging scenarios are coming from all stakeholders. But a recent incident in Saravan county in Sistan-Baluchestan, close to the Pakistan border, has also drawn attention to the Iran-Pakistan border region. This has broadened the debate over the Gulf region’s security and evolving geopolitics, and Pakistan’s role in it. The incident was reported on Sept 12, when heavy fighting between Iranian security forces and unidentified gunmen spread across parts of Saravan, with reports of attacks on military vehicles and dozens of security personnel killed or wounded. Although the identity of the armed group is not yet clear, some analysts have attributed the attack to Jaish al-Adl or the People’s Fighters Front, an alliance of several groups, reportedly including Jaish al-Adl. Since the start of the conflict in West Asia, Balochistan’s security dynamics have changed. The conflict has altered the operating environment in which an existing insurgency was already functioning. The BLA and other allied groups have intensified theirterrorist activities. The economic blockade announced by these groups has disrupted transportation and halted economic activity, particularly in the mineral sector. Theclosure of the frontier with Afghanistanand the partial closure of the border with Iran have contributed to the crisis. Taken together, these developments have affected the region’s security, internal political dynamics and geopolitical environment, bringing new risks to the province. An angle that has largely been overlooked in the broader conflict theatre in this area is the state of affairs along the Pakistan-Iran border, which stretches for around 900 kilometres and where multiple violent religious and nationalist insurgent groups, as well as transnational criminal networks, operate. The border’s porous nature raises further security concerns. According to media reports, Pakistani security institutions had placed Balochistan on high alert because of the possible fallout from the Iran war. The situation along the Pakistan-Iran border in the broader conflict has been largely overlooked. The Jan 16, 2024,Iranian strike inside Pakistan, allegedly targeting Jaish al-Adl hideouts, followed by Pakistan’s retaliatory strikes on militant targets in Iran, changed the dynamics of their bilateral relations and prompted greater security cooperation. That cooperation has largely remained intact. However, the recent Saravan attack has raised questions about how the changing regional environment could affect the future course of frontier security, particularly as Pakistan’s border with Afghanistan remains closed and Iran is an alternative, although very expensive, route for transnational trade. For Iran, if the Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) has to concentrate its resources on US and Israeli strikes, the Strait of Hormuz and operations in the Gulf, Sistan-Baluchestan could become a peripheral theatre competing for Iranian security resources. Any escalation of tensions between Iran and Pakistan is in neither country’s interest. However, non-state actors always try to find an opportunity in evolving conflicts, especially when wider regional contexts provide them with more meaning and relevance in the conflict theatre. The BLA and other insurgent groups appear to have viewed the war as an opportunity to escalate their operations, perhaps hoping that they could eventually be considered as potential proxies against Iran, as happened in Syria with America’s partnership with the Syrian Democratic Forces. The SDF was a coalition that included Kurdish armed groups such as the YPG and YPJ, along with Syrian Arab and Assyrian/ Christian elements. The BLA has also issued a few statements supporting US strikes on Iran. Perhaps the BLA believes it can find meaning in the wider conflict in West Asia. Still, the BLA is missing a point in its calculation: the convergence of US, Pakistani, and Saudi geopolitical and strategic interests will persist in the coming years. At the same time, Jaish al-Adl and several smaller groups have reportedly sought to broaden their activities against the Quds Force and IRGC. The group remained relatively quiet until Iranian security forces launched an operation against suspected terrorists in Saravan last August, reportedly apprehending several Jaish al-Adl members and killing one. During the operation, security forces said they recovered a significant arsenal of military hardware, including dozens of Kalashnikov automatic rifles, hand grenades, RPG-7 launchers, around 20 kilograms of C-4 military-grade explosives, 150 rounds of ammunition, and several Starlink satellite internet devices. The Saravan operation reported last week has since been interpreted in multiple ways, mostly based on assumptions rather than established evidence. One popular theory links the attack to the intensification of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia. The incident also occurred while Pakistan was diplomatically engaged with Iran. According to a media report, subsequently denied by Pakistan, Islamabad had conveyed a Saudi message to Tehran asking Iran to restrain the Houthis. A popular perception in the border region of Balochistan is that if Iran can use the Houthis as a proxy against Saudi Arabia, it must also expect the possibility of a similar reaction from Saudi Arabia. The Sunni militias operating in Sistan-Baluchestan, from Jundullah to the People’s Fighters Front, are said to be proxies of foreign powers including the US and Saudi Arabia. That perception is nurturing new theories. A few of them are critical of Pakistan too. Whether such perceptions translate into an actual Saudi strategy is another question. But perceptions themselves can influence the behaviour of armed groups and local actors, particularly in a region where terrorist networks, cross-border tribal connections and informal economic networks overlap. Beyond all the theories surrounding the strategic calculus of West Asia and the prospects of Saudi proxies emerging along the Pakistan-Iran border, one fact remains clear: Pakistan cannot afford further chaos in the border region of Balochistan. Any expansion of the regional conflict in an already fragile security environment could make the country’s internal security dynamics considerably more complex.
articles.author: Muhammad Amir Rana

articles.title: A small republic in every classroom
articles.content: PAKISTAN is extraordinarily young. Two in every three of its people are under 30. The question is not whether Generation Z will change Pakistan. Demographically, it will. The question is whether it will be ready, and little in the way this country is arranged suggests it will. Their task can be stated in a sentence. The Constitution of Pakistan on paper and the Constitution as it works on the ground are two different documents, and the distance between them is what this generation has to close. I was 14 when martial law came and a young man when that general died. My generation learnt a dangerous lesson: power does not explain itself. The man who speaks out is transferred; the man who stays quiet is promoted; the judge who insists upon his independence is superseded. Caution, practised long enough, becomes accommodation, and accommodation becomes submission. We learnt to accommodate power. Our institutions learnt it too. The courts found a doctrine for every occasion: revolutionary legality in 1958, necessity in 1977, validation in 2000. Havel wrote of the greengrocer who displayed a slogan he did not believe because it was safer. Parties became family enterprises; student unions were banned in 1984 and never restored. What we built governs without consent. Pakistan’s next generation will not be formed by protest. It will be formed by argument, and the place to begin it already exists. So what must this generation build first? Not a movement. Character. I have watched men who stood fearlessly at the bar change after reaching the bench. Not suddenly, and not for money. The comfort of office begins quietly to weigh, and each surrender is called realistic. Character is what resists that, and character is built by exposure to lives larger than one’s own. That is what history, literature and poetry are for: to make suffering legible, so that conviction has something to rest upon. But reading alone will not do it. What is read must be argued about, and the structure for that argument is already built, already funded and sitting idle. It is the university classroom. Every class, in every discipline, should be run as a small republic, and the argument should be about the discipline itself. Let the law class argue whether a judgement was rightly decided, not merely what it held. Let the medical class argue triage, consent, and who receives the last bed in a public ward. Let the engineering class argue what was built, who paid, and who must live beside it. Let the business class argue what a wage ought to be, and whether a balance sheet that is lawful is therefore honest. Every syllabus buries such questions beneath what is examinable. Let each class elect its office bearers, for a fixed term and with real duties. Let the elections be contested, and let students lose them, because losing an election and returning next week to sit beside the person who beat you is the most useful hour of civic instruction this country could offer. Let the dissenter be protected by rule, not by the goodwill of the majority. That is how a democratic mind is made: by being outvoted by someone you believe wrong, and having to work beside him afterwards. Argue any of these questions honestly and it will not remain within its discipline. Ask an engineering class whether the dam should be built. The answer requires a lawyer on water rights, an economist on who bears the cost, a doctor on what happens downstream, and someone who has met the people being moved. A faculty can contain a syllabus; it cannot contain a real question. Memorisation keeps a student inside his discipline; argument drives him out. Debate and multidisciplinary education are not two reforms but one, and the first produces the second. This is also where the politics lies. Our professions are organised as separate estates: a bar, a medical association, a chamber of commerce. Each can be managed on its own. What cannot be managed is a generation of doctors, engineers, lawyers and accountants who argued with one another at 20 and still take one another’s calls at 40. Teaching without debate is not education. It is transmission. Education here needs revisiting at its root: less theory recited, more of it tested against the country outside. Take the law class to a district court, the medical class to a public ward at night, the engineering class to the settlement beside the project, the business class to the factory floor. Students must be made to feel Pakistan and its misery, not to read about it. Imagine the young men and women such an education would prepare. The more grounded they are, the more effective they will be. A generation formed this way will not need to be told to push back against unelected power. It will be too many, too competent and too well connected to be governed without consent. None of this arrives quickly. It takes two decades, the time between losing a class election at 20 and running a ministry or a court at 40. That is the honest horizon, and why the work must begin now. Return, then, to the gap. On paper the Constitution is not in doubt: authority exercised through the chosen representatives of the people, rights that power may not violate, public power exercised for the common good. My generation learnt to live inside the distance between that page and this country. Look at what we have brought it to. Closing that distance is the work now left to theirs. They must learn to hold power to account. It begins in a classroom, with an argument, and an election that somebody loses. The writer is a former senior puisne judge of the Supreme Court of Pakistan. He holds the Distinguished Chair in Constitutionalism & Justice at the Shaikh Ahmad Hassan School of Law, Lums, and is currently a Distinguished Visiting Fellow at Yale University.
articles.author: Justice (retd) Syed Mansoor Ali Shah

articles.title: No neutral ground
articles.content: NOBODY says ‘I am not complicit’ unless the question has already crossed their mind. Singer Ed Sheeran wrote it this week, unprompted, in a statement captioned “It’s important that I set out some facts.” Not facts about Gaza, where the death toll had passed 73,000 by the night of his opening act, but facts about himself. The sequence matters. On Sept 4, in New Jersey, the rapper Macklemore performed Hind’s Hall, a song named for the Columbia University building that students renamed for Hind Rajab, a five-year-old killed in Gaza. He told the crowd he had wanted this tour so he could stand in stadiums and say two words near to his heart. Free Palestine. The next night he said them again, and added that criticism of Israel was not criticism of Jews. On Sept 6, the Israeli-American Council launched a petition to remove him. On Sept 11, the singer Pink amplified the calls. On Sept 14, the promoter announced he was off the tour, after Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium, said he would not be welcome there and, by Macklemore’s account, rallied other stadium owners to do the same. There is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed. I want to be careful here, because I am writing from a country where the calculation he made is not unusual and the stakes are considerably higher. We know what it costs to say certain things. We know which sentences require a call to an editor first, which ones get a piece held, which subjects are approached through metaphor or not at all. I could give you a list. I am not going to, and you already know why, and the fact that you know is the whole point. Every journalist reading this in Pakistan has a version of that list, and none of us wrote it down. So, I recognise the shape of what Sheeran did. The calculation is familiar. What is not familiar is the price. Nobody threatened him. No one was going to arrest him or disappear him or shut down his tour for saying that children should not be killed. The worst that could happen was that some stadium owners would be angry and some ticket sales would suffer. That is the entire risk he was weighing. Ten days of silence bought against that. There is something clarifying about watching the same instinct operate where the danger is so much smaller. It tells you the instinct is not really about danger. When he did speak, on Sept 15, it was to explain that the decision had not been his. He had spent the week building bridges. The venues and the promoter had decided. He respects Macklemore’s strength of purpose, but there is room for multiple approaches to peace. He chooses to use his platform as a place of safety and sanctuary, to keep conversations open rather than closed. His fans, he said, do not come to his shows expecting a political forum. Within hours, the rest of his line-up was gone. Aaron Rowe went first, then Finneas, Lukas Graham and the band Beoga, who had been playing a six-song set with Sheeran every night. Two of them reached for Irish history to explain themselves. Colonialism, famine, occupation. We are Irish people who understand these things, Beoga said. People who have been on the receiving end of an empire tend to recognise the machinery faster. It is not a superior moral instinct. It is just familiarity. Here is the part worth sitting with. It was not Macklemore’s removal that emptied the tour. He was dropped on the 14th and the line-up held. What broke it was Sheeran’s explanation on the 15th. The defence of neutrality was the thing that made neutrality impossible for everyone else on the bill. The Israeli-American Council, which essentially got what it wanted, then turned on Sheeran too. It is his stage, they said, his tour carries his name, and so the responsibility is his. On that single point they are right, and they are saying what Macklemore said in different words: there is no neutral position between the oppressor and the oppressed. When both sides find your neutrality contemptible, that is information. On Wednesday, Macklemore said he would donate the entire $1 million he earned from those two nights to six organisations working in Gaza, and invited Robert Kraft to match it. Kraft representatives declined to comment. In the same post, Macklemore made a point of naming the organisers and activists who have paid real costs for standing with Palestine, noting that their risk is of an order far different to his own. Three men were asked the same question this month. One paid $1m to answer it. One declined to comment. One called his stage a sanctuary. A sanctuary is defined by who is allowed inside it. So, who was this one for? The writer is a journalist and conducts writing workshops in Karachi.
articles.author: Muna Khan

articles.title: Celebrating victory
articles.content: PAKISTAN has lived with conflict for much of its existence. Its security concerns are real, and its armed forces have repeatedly demonstrated courage. Yet conflict also teaches one that enduring security depends not only on responding to challenges, but on creating conditions in which they do not arise again. This is worth keeping in mind as Pakistan develops new traditions of commemorating military achievements. On May 10 this year, the country observed the first anniversary of Marka-i-Haq, commemorating Operation Bunyanum Marsoos. The government has announced that May 10 will be observed annually as Marka-i-Haq Day. The anniversary was marked by official ceremonies and patriotic events. Transforming a short, dangerous military confrontation into an annual celebration may not necessarily serve Pakistan’s long-term interests. In nuclearised South Asia, perhaps victory is best accompanied by humility. Any confrontation that ends without a decisive settlement reminds us how quickly events can move towards escalation. Preparedness is most valuable when accompanied by reflection, restraint and diplomacy. The purpose of national strength remains the preservation of peace. Pakistan already has another strategic commemoration Youm-i-Takbeer that is observed on May 28 to mark the 1998 nuclear tests. The nuclear deterrent was of historic significance and altered Pakistan’s security calculus. Yet nuclear capability primarily serves deterrence, ensuring that nuclear weapons never have to be used. A nuclear state needs restraint, sound command and control and crisis management. Perhaps observances could be brought together. Then comes Defence Day on Sept 6, when the nation remembers the sacrifices of the 1965 war. Perhaps all these observances could be brought together, honouring sacrifices and victories on this single solemn occasion while remembering the human cost of conflict and the importance of peace. This perspective also lends significance to the inauguration of Yadgar-i-Fatah in Islamabad on the eve of Independence Day. Memorials to fallen soldiers are a natural way for nations to remember sacrifice. But national symbols also acquire meaning from the occasions on which they are presented to the public. Independence Day provides an opportunity to look beyond the events that shaped our statehood and ask how successfully we have fulfilled its larger promise. Our independence was born in great human suffering. Millions were displaced and hundreds of thousands lost their lives. Since then, Pakistan has experienced wars, political upheavals, economic crises, terrorism and institutional difficulties. Considerable ground remains to be covered. Aug 14 can therefore be more than a patriotic celebration. It can invite an assessment of national performance. What progress have we made in education, health, justice, governance and human development? Why do so many young Pakistanis continue to look overseas for opportunities? Such questions are not a departure from patriotism, they are expressions of it. Security has several dimensions. Military preparedness remains essential, but sustainable national security also depends on economic strength, political stability, institutional resilience and diplomatic space. Pakistan faces debt, unemployment, inadequate public services and limited fiscal space. Defence is a national priority, but resources are finite and every expenditure carries an opportunity cost. A confident nation can celebrate its soldiers while recognising its scientists, teachers, entrepreneurs, athletes, artists, doctors and civil servants. National pride can come not only from defending territory, but also from educating children, providing justice and building institutions. The recent Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek offered a reminder of the regional environment. Pakistan and India were represented by their prime ministers, but the encounter produced little visible thaw. Yet the SCO remains a forum for engagement on counterterrorism, trade and economic cooperation. Pakistan’s assumption of the SCO chair offers an opportunity to demonstrate that defending national interests and seeking regional stability need not be competing objectives. Pakistan should honour its martyrs, remember military successes, maintain effective defence and preserve a credible deterrent. At the same time, the larger national aspiration must remain a Pakistan that is economically strong, politically stable, institutionally mature and diplomatically confident. We need neither forget our victories nor become defined by them. A nation can honour its soldiers without glorifying war, remember sacrifice without perpetuating confrontation, and maintain deterrence while pursuing the peace and prosperity that give national strength its deepest meaning. The writer is a former IGP Punjab and a former Punjab caretaker home minister.
articles.author: Shaukat Javed

articles.title: Kohat attack
articles.content: FRIDAY’Sattack in Kohatmarks a further escalation by Pakistan’s enemies. They targeted a mosque in Kohat’s old Police Lines with an explosives-laden vehicle, then attempted to storm the compound and attack police facilities in the ensuing chaos. At least 23, including 17 police personnel and officials, weremartyredin this dastardly assault on worshippers. More than 100 were wounded. But police and security forces regrouped quickly and launched a valiant counterassault, eliminating all but two of the attackers within hours of the initial bombing. The remaining two were neutralised in a clean-up operation that extended overnight, supervised by some of the top police and counterterrorism officials, with one holed-up terrorist killed and the other blowing themselves up rather than face the consequences of their actions. The operation produced considerable acts of courage, not least by the additional inspector-general of the CTD, who was injured by a grenade yet returned to conclude the clean-up. The nation will mourn the lives lost and pray for those who were injured. The nation will also demand swift justice for those who lost loved ones. The group which claimed the attack has, by attacking worshippers on what Muslims consider the holiest occasion of the week, not only shown that it observes no ethical limits, but also that it is operating with a single goal: to cause maximum bloodshed and harm. The Ittehadul Mujahideen, an umbrella organisation of terrorist outfits, is, according to the Jamestown Foundation think tank, believed to operate from safe havens across the border, share intelligence and coordinate attacks with its terrorist factions, and run organised digital campaigns. It has apparently used drone technologies to deadly effect while targeting security forces and installations in the past. As such, it is considered in some circles to be a more serious and sophisticated threat than the TTP. It needs to be treated as such. The KP police must be better equipped and trained. They are facing an enemy which is increasingly using modern technology to cause bloodshed. They must be supported with the equipment, strategies and technologies they need to effectively limit and counter the constant, deadly threat they face. Simultaneously, the authorities need to review the approaches being taken to counter violent actors. National policy on counterterrorism requires recalibration and revisiting, especially regarding its diplomatic, political and social aspects, which must be addressed together to secure stable dividends. Sadly, the public’s attention is so fixated on social, political and economic problems that the terrorism crisis has been pushed to the margins of national discourse. Pakistan must confront these networks with the full force of the state and the law, but cannot do so effectively till its own house is in order.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Beyond fossils
articles.content: PAKISTAN’S vulnerability to external energy shocks is no secret. The ongoing disruptions of LNG supplies caused by the Middle East conflict have only reinforced that as well as the risks to an economy dependent on imported energy. If anything, the current crisis should force a rethink of the country’s energy policy. Pakistan must accelerate the transition to renewables to reduce its vulnerability to imported fuels. This is exactly what the latest Gastech Conference report has suggested. The rooftop-solar boom has shown what consumer initiative can achieve. Thousands of homes and businesses have installed systems to reduce reliance on expensive grid electricity, increasing distributed generation and helping lower daytime consumption during the summer cooling season. This has been particularly useful amid disrupted LNG supplies. The government should build on this consumer-led transition. The next phase, however, must be better designed. Solar panels alone cannot resolve our energy woes. Their output falls sharply after sunset, when household demand rises, especially in summer. Without storage, the grid remains dependent on gas and other fossil fuels to meet evening peaks. Government incentives should therefore increasingly support solar-plus-storage systems. Affordable financing, targeted tax relief and easier access to batteries will encourage households and businesses to store surplus daytime electricity for use at night. The policy must also address equity. Households able to afford solar systems can reduce their reliance on the grid, while poorer consumers may continue to bear a disproportionate share of fixed network costs. A poorly managed transition will deepen this divide. The government must ensure that the benefits of decentralised generation are not limited to those with substantial upfront capital. One way to broaden access is to encourage small, home-based neighbourhood solar grids. Households with surplus electricity and battery capacity could supply nearby consumers under regulated arrangements. This would allow power to be generated, stored and consumed closer to where it is needed. Reducing fossil-fuel dependence also has important economic implications. Greater use of domestic renewable resources can reduce exposure to volatile global prices and shipping disruptions while conserving foreign exchange. For an economy repeatedly facing external financing pressures, this is especially important.
